query: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy previously showed limited amorphous retention and a complicated thermal response. Earlier thermal studies of Ni–P and Pd–Ni–P alloys found that rapid quenching could produce amorphous material, but that its stability was limited during subsequent heating. The design challenge is therefore to obtain robust glass formation across relevant cooling conditions without sacrificing stability during reheating. What single intervention could improve amorphous retention and thermal stability during solidification and thermal analysis? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the reported behavior of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, the cooling-rate and reheating conditions under which it should or should not succeed, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a ≈1 at% addition of a large atomic radius element like gadolinium (Gd) into the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy will improve its amorphous retention and thermal stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy produced by arc melting exhibiting limited amorphous retention and complex, multi‐phase crystallization during both solidification and reheating.
generation.intervention: Micro‐alloying with approximately 1 at% Gd added to the base alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied during conventional solidification processes (e.g., melt spinning with cooling rates on the order of 10^5–10^6 K/s) and under thermal analysis conditions that include reheating at moderate rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local atomic disorder and packing frustration caused by the large atomic size difference of Gd compared to the base elements.
generation.mechanism: The presence of a small amount of Gd is expected to introduce additional strain and geometric frustration in the melt due to its atomic size mismatch. This increased disorder kinetically retards nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during rapid cooling and reduces the tendency for crystallization during subsequent thermal cycling (reheating), thereby stabilizing the amorphous phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the pristine Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, the Gd-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit a broader processing window for glass formation—forming a more uniform amorphous structure during rapid quenching—and will show delayed or suppressed crystallization upon reheating, as evidenced by shifts in characteristic DSC exotherms and a more diffuse XRD pattern.
generation.baseline: The original Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy displays limited amorphous retention with multiple crystallization peaks during DSC analyses and clearly defined crystalline phases upon slow cooling.
generation.boundary: This intervention might be ineffective if (a) the Gd concentration is significantly lower than ≈1 at%, (b) the cooling rates deviate from the ultrafast regime, or (c) the reheating conditions exceed temperatures where even enhanced frustration cannot kinetically hinder crystallization.
generation.uncertainty: Although micro‐alloying with Gd has shown marked effects in simpler Pd–Ni–P systems, its exact impact on the multi‐component Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni–P alloy remains to be quantified; the relative size, mixing enthalpy, and interaction with P in this system introduce some uncertainty regarding the magnitude of the improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 and one set modified with ~1 at% Gd. Subject both sets to identical rapid quenching conditions (e.g., melt spinning with cooling rates between 10^5 and 10^6 K/s). Then, perform differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the extent of amorphization and crystallization behavior during reheating.
measurements: DSC to determine crystallization onset temperatures and exothermic peak intensities
XRD to evaluate the breadth and intensity of the amorphous halo versus crystalline peaks
TEM for direct microstructural observation of amorphous versus crystalline domains
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Gd-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant shift in crystallization onset temperature, reduction in exothermic peak intensity, or improvements in amorphous microstructural uniformity (as compared to the baseline alloy), then the hypothesis that Gd addition improves amorphous retention and thermal stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. To investigate the impact of small concentrations of an additionally added element on a glass-forming alloy, the critical cooling rates and glass formation regions are computed for the Pd-Ni-P-system micro-alloyed with 1 at% of Co, Cu, Fe, and Gd. Micro-alloying of Co, Cu, and Fe had little effect on the overall glass-forming ability which matches well with experimental results for (Pd40Ni40P20)99Co1 and (Pd40Ni40P20)99.4Fe0.6 that showed an impact on the mechanical properties without affecting the glass formation properties in a significant way (see Figure 6) [,]. This behavior is to be expected within the framework of the current model since cobalt, copper, and iron are similar in atomic weight and radius to nickel and therefore will not impact the calculation. This is different for gadolinium, since it varies in its properties significantly from the former alloying elements. The impact of the micro-alloying of gadolinium is even noticeable for concentrations below 1 at% as shown in Figure 6 within the employed model.
